Explain in your own words what 'Centrifugation and Its Types' refers to.
questions.a: Spinning samples around an axis lets centrifugal force sort particles by density: differential centrifugation exploits differing sedimentation rates to drop nuclei, mitochondria or chloroplasts in turn, density-gradient runs settle molecules at levels matching their densities inside a preformed gradient, and ultracentrifugation pushes past one hundred thousand times gravity to separate dissolved molecules.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Centrifugation and Its Types'.
questions.a: Rate of sedimentation sorts by size and density in differential runs; a gradient sorts similar-sized particles purely by density.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Centrifugation and Its Types' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Electrophoresis of DNA and Proteins' refers to.
questions.a: An electric field walks charged macromolecules through a gel at speeds set by their charge-to-size ratio: negatively charged DNA threads from the wells toward the anode with short pieces outrunning long ones across an 80-120 volt run, while SDS coats proteins uniformly negative so polyacrylamide gels - loose at 4-8 percent for big proteins, hard at 12-20 percent for small ones - resolve them, with bromophenol blue racing ahead as the tracking dye and ethidium bromide or Coomassie blue making the bands visible.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Electrophoresis of DNA and Proteins'.
questions.a: DNA sorts by size alone toward the anode; SDS-PAGE sorts proteins by size after the detergent equalises their charge.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Electrophoresis of DNA and Proteins' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: ELISA Formats for Antigen and Antibody

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'ELISA Formats for Antigen and Antibody' refers to.
questions.a: Engvall and Perlman's 1971 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay quantifies antigen or antibody through an enzyme's colour signal: direct ELISA coats antigen and adds one labelled antibody; indirect adds an unlabelled primary then a labelled secondary for extra sensitivity; sandwich traps antigen between a captured and a second labelled antibody for high specificity; and competitive ELISA reads antigen amounts inversely, more antigen meaning weaker colour.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'ELISA Formats for Antigen and Antibody'.
questions.a: Count the antibodies and which one carries the enzyme - that tells you the format and what the colour measures.

questions.q: Under which section is 'ELISA Formats for Antigen and Antibody' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Chromatography Modes from Adsorption to Gas

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Chromatography Modes from Adsorption to Gas' refers to.
questions.a: Chromatography races solutes between a moving eluent and a held stationary phase, each molecule eluting in step with its affinity: adsorption onto polar surfaces, partitioning between immiscible solvents, ion-exchange electrostatics, molecular sieving in gel filtration, biospecific ligand capture in affinity columns, high-pressure liquid runs through fine particles, and gas chromatography for volatiles - all traced as peaks on a chromatogram.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Chromatography Modes from Adsorption to Gas'.
questions.a: Name the mode by what holds the solute back - surface, solvent, charge, pore, ligand, pressure or volatility.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Chromatography Modes from Adsorption to Gas' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: FISH, Microarray and Flow Cytometry Profiling

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'FISH, Microarray and Flow Cytometry Profiling' refers to.
questions.a: Three probes-on-cells techniques close the toolkit: fluorescent in situ hybridisation anneals a labelled DNA probe to its chromosome site and even paints every chromosome a different colour; DNA microarrays hybridise Cy3/Cy5-labelled cDNA onto thousands of immobilised probes to flag upregulated and downregulated genes; and flow cytometry streams single cells past lasers - a Coulter-counter idea from the late 1950s - reading scattered and fluorescent light to count and sort labelled populations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'FISH, Microarray and Flow Cytometry Profiling'.
questions.a: Label the probe or the cell, let complementarity or a laser do the sorting, and read the colours as biology.

questions.q: Under which section is 'FISH, Microarray and Flow Cytometry Profiling' taught, and from which source text?
